options.text: Isometric exercise, contracting the muscle without moving the joint
options.rationale: Builds static strength and joint stability and is safe around painful or healing tissue.

questions.takeaway: Isotonic moves the joint. Isometric does not, which is why it works in a limb that must stay still.

questions.stem: Which factors influence a patient's level of activity? Select all that apply.

options.text: Environment
options.rationale: Stairs, terrain, and access decide what movement is possible.

options.text: Social support
options.rationale: Determines whether someone has help and encouragement to stay active.

options.text: Developmental stage
options.rationale: Named among the influences on activity. What is expected differs across the lifespan.

options.text: Blood type
options.rationale: Has no relationship to activity or mobility.

options.text: Culture
options.rationale: Shapes which activities are valued and considered appropriate.

questions.takeaway: Activity is shaped by development, health status, lifestyle, culture, environment, behavior, and social support.

questions.stem: A patient recovering from pneumonia has been in bed for four days. Which action best prevents respiratory complications of immobility?

options.text: Assist the patient to sit upright and cough and deep breathe
options.rationale: Sitting upright increases lung expansion and coughing clears retained secretions, which are the two failures behind atelectasis.

options.text: Apply sequential compression devices to both legs
options.rationale: Prevents venous stasis and thrombus. It does nothing for the lungs.

options.text: Perform passive range of motion to all extremities
options.rationale: Prevents contractures. Correct care, different system.

options.text: Increase dietary protein intake
options.rationale: Addresses negative nitrogen balance, not lung expansion.

questions.takeaway: Match the intervention to the mechanism. Secretions pooling needs expansion and coughing.

questions.stem: A patient on bed rest for four days is preparing to ambulate. Supine blood pressure is 128/76 with a pulse of 78. After sitting at the edge of the bed for one minute, blood pressure is 102/58 with a pulse of 104 and the patient reports the room is spinning. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Assist the patient to stand so the episode resolves with movement
options.rationale: Standing raises the head further above the heart and deepens the drop in cerebral perfusion. This is the moment a fall happens.

options.text: Keep the patient sitting and supported, then recheck before standing
options.rationale: A drop in pressure with a compensating rise in rate on sitting is orthostatic hypotension. Staying seated lets the circulation catch up without abandoning the activity, and the recheck is the checkpoint before the riskiest part.

options.text: Return the patient to supine and cancel activity for the day
options.rationale: Abandoning the activity treats the symptom by deepening the deconditioning that caused it.

options.text: Administer the ordered analgesic and reattempt in one hour
options.rationale: Nothing in the findings describes pain, and an hour of additional rest does not improve orthostatic tolerance.

questions.takeaway: Read the pair together: falling pressure with a rising rate on position change is orthostatic hypotension. Stage the change, do not cancel it.

questions.stem: A patient has been immobile for five days after a pelvic fracture. The nurse notes that the left calf is 3 cm larger than the right and is warm and tender. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Apply the sequential compression devices to both legs
options.rationale: Compression prevents venous stasis in a limb without a clot. Applying it now treats prevention as if it were treatment.

options.text: Encourage active ankle pumping in both legs every hour
options.rationale: Leg exercises are correct prevention and are not the response to a limb that already shows the complication.

options.text: Hold the sequential compression devices and notify the provider
options.rationale: Unilateral calf swelling with warmth and tenderness suggests a thrombus has already formed. Compression on a limb with a suspected clot is applied only after evaluation, so the device is held and the finding is reported.

options.text: Measure both calves again in four hours to establish a trend
options.rationale: The difference is already measured and symptomatic. Waiting adds risk without adding information.

questions.takeaway: Prevention and treatment are different. Once one limb shows swelling, warmth, and tenderness, stop preventing and start reporting.

questions.stem: A patient who slides down in bed several times a day has an area of reddened, partially denuded skin over the sacrum. The bed is routinely kept at 45 degrees. Which change most directly addresses the mechanism causing this injury?

options.text: Apply a moisture barrier ointment to the sacrum twice daily
options.rationale: Moisture management is appropriate skin care and does nothing about the sliding that is tearing tissue.

options.text: Turn the patient every two hours without changing the bed angle
options.rationale: Turning limits time under pressure. The injury here is produced by sliding, which continues at 45 degrees.

options.text: Place a pillow under the knees to improve comfort
options.rationale: Knee flexion does help resist sliding, and alone it does not address either the bed angle or how the patient is moved.

options.text: Lower the head of the bed when clinically possible and use a lift sheet to reposition
options.rationale: Elevation lets the skeleton slide while the skin stays fixed, which is shear, and dragging adds friction. Lowering the angle removes the driving force and lifting removes the surface drag.

questions.takeaway: Pressure pushes down, friction rubs, shear slides the tissue under fixed skin. A head-up bed plus dragging produces the last two.

questions.stem: A patient immobile for two weeks has a footboard in place. The nurse finds the feet resting with the toes pointed and a gap of several inches between the soles and the board. Which conclusion does the nurse draw?

options.text: The device is not in contact with the feet, so it is not preventing plantar flexion
options.rationale: A footboard works only when the soles rest against it at a neutral angle. A gap means the ankles are free to settle into plantar flexion, which is how foot drop develops.

options.text: The findings are expected and the device is working as intended
options.rationale: Toes pointed is the position the device exists to prevent, so the finding is evidence it is not working.

options.text: The patient has developed a permanent contracture that the device can now correct
options.rationale: Contractures are permanent shortening. Positioning prevents them and does not reverse them, and nothing here establishes one has formed yet.

options.text: The gap indicates the patient has been performing active ankle exercises
options.rationale: Active movement would show the ankles in varied positions, not both settled in plantar flexion.

questions.takeaway: A supportive device only works in contact. Check that the intervention is actually happening, not just present.

questions.stem: A patient immobile for three weeks eats about a third of each meal. Serum albumin has fallen from 3.8 to 2.9 g/dL, weight is down 4 kg, and the arms and legs appear visibly thinner. Which process best explains this pattern?

options.text: Fluid volume deficit producing the weight loss
options.rationale: Dehydration would raise albumin through hemoconcentration rather than lower it, and it does not thin the extremities.

options.text: Negative nitrogen balance from immobility compounded by reduced intake
options.rationale: Immobility drives protein breakdown beyond intake, and decreased appetite is itself a listed metabolic effect. Falling albumin with visible loss of lean mass is that process made measurable.

options.text: Increased metabolic demand from prolonged bed rest
options.rationale: Immobility lowers metabolic demand. The direction is reversed.

options.text: Altered calcium metabolism causing muscle wasting
options.rationale: Altered calcium metabolism produces bone demineralization and a rising serum calcium, not loss of muscle protein.

questions.takeaway: Immobility takes protein apart while appetite falls. Albumin down, weight down, limbs thinner is one process, not three.

questions.stem: A patient two days after knee arthroplasty is on a weight-bearing restriction and reports the knee is too painful to bend beyond a few degrees. Which exercise best maintains quadriceps strength now?

options.text: Perform straight leg raises through the full range
options.rationale: Isotonic work through a full arc. The hip moves and the load on a painful healing knee exceeds what this patient tolerates.

options.text: Have the nurse move the knee through its full range twice daily
options.rationale: Passive range maintains flexibility and the patient's muscle does no work, so no strength is built.

options.text: Tighten the quadriceps and hold without moving the knee
options.rationale: Isometric contraction loads the muscle with no joint movement, which is why it is used around painful or healing joints. Strength and joint stability are preserved during the period the knee cannot move.

options.text: Walk short distances with a walker several times daily
options.rationale: Isotonic and appropriate later. It conflicts with the weight-bearing restriction stated in the stem.

questions.takeaway: Isotonic moves the joint, isometric does not. When the joint cannot move, isometric is the only way to keep the muscle.

questions.stem: A nurse repositions an immobile patient from supine to a 30-degree side-lying position with pillows supporting the back, between the knees, and under the upper arm. Which outcomes does this positioning achieve? Select all that apply.

options.text: Maintains body alignment
options.rationale: Support at the back, knees, and arm holds the trunk and limbs in alignment instead of letting them collapse into the mattress.

options.text: Reduces pressure over the sacrum
options.rationale: Turning shifts weight off the tissue that was bearing it, which limits time under load.

options.text: Prevents hip and knee contracture by holding the joints out of fixed flexion
options.rationale: A pillow between the knees keeps the upper leg from adducting and the hips from settling into a fixed position.

options.text: Supports lung expansion compared with a flat supine position
options.rationale: Position determines how far the lungs can expand, and a supported side-lying position relieves pressure on the dependent lung compared with lying flat.

options.text: Eliminates the need for scheduled range-of-motion exercises
options.rationale: Position and movement do different jobs. Holding a joint correctly does not carry it through its arc.

options.text: Restores muscle strength lost during the period of bed rest
options.rationale: Strength returns with loading and activity. No position rebuilds muscle.

questions.takeaway: Positioning maintains alignment, supports breathing, protects skin, promotes comfort, prevents contractures, supports function. It does not replace movement.

questions.stem: A patient with cerebral edema after a closed head injury has a serum sodium of 118 mEq/L and is becoming drowsy. Which IV solution does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: 3% sodium chloride
options.rationale: A hypertonic solution has a higher osmolarity than plasma, so it pulls water out of cells and into the bloodstream. Severe hyponatremia and cerebral edema are both listed indications for hypertonic saline, and pulling water into the vasculature lowers intracranial pressure while raising the sodium.

options.text: 0.45% sodium chloride
options.rationale: A hypotonic solution is more dilute than plasma, so water shifts into cells and they swell. This is the option that looks right because it is saline.

options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride
options.rationale: An isotonic solution matches plasma osmolarity, so there is no net water movement across cell membranes. It expands volume, which is a different problem from the one in the stem.

options.text: 5% dextrose in water
options.rationale: D5W is isotonic in the bag and becomes hypotonic once the dextrose is metabolized, leaving free water. This is among the worst choices here despite appearing on the isotonic list.

questions.takeaway: Hypertonic solutions pull water out of cells. That single action is why the same fluid treats severe hyponatremia and cerebral edema at once.

questions.stem: A patient with diabetic ketoacidosis has completed initial fluid resuscitation with 0.9% sodium chloride and is now hemodynamically stable with a blood pressure of 118 over 70. Which solution does the nurse anticipate for continued maintenance fluid?

options.text: 3% sodium chloride
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline pulls water out of cells into the vasculature and is reserved for severe hyponatremia and cerebral edema. The osmotic diuresis of ketoacidosis has already dehydrated the cells, so pulling more water out would worsen the deficit.

options.text: 0.45% sodium chloride
options.rationale: Half normal saline is hypotonic, so water shifts into cells by osmosis and rehydrates them. Diabetic ketoacidosis after initial resuscitation is a named indication for hypotonic fluid, because the vascular space has been filled and the cellular dehydration remains.

options.text: 10% dextrose in water
options.rationale: D10W is hypertonic and is used for hypoglycemia. Adding concentrated dextrose at this stage works against the treatment, and dextrose is added later only once glucose falls to a target.

options.text: Lactated Ringer's
options.rationale: Lactated Ringer's is isotonic and produces no net water shift across cell membranes. Continuing it maintains volume without addressing the cellular dehydration that remains.

questions.takeaway: Hypotonic fluids move water into cells, which is why they follow rather than lead resuscitation in ketoacidosis. Fill the vascular space first, then rehydrate the cells.

questions.stem: A nursing student asks why 5% dextrose in water is not used to resuscitate a patient in hemorrhagic shock even though it appears on the isotonic list. Which response is correct?

options.text: It contains too much dextrose and will cause the blood to clot in the tubing
options.rationale: Clotting in the line is a concern with lactated Ringer's during a transfusion because it contains calcium. That is a transfusion rule, not the reason it fails as a resuscitation fluid.

options.text: It is hypertonic and would pull fluid out of the cells the patient needs to hydrate
options.rationale: Hypertonic solutions have osmolarity above plasma and shrink cells. This option has the direction and the classification both reversed.

options.text: It is isotonic in the bag, and once the dextrose is metabolized the remaining free water moves into cells
options.rationale: Tonicity describes the solution compared with plasma at the moment of infusion. The dextrose is taken up and metabolized, leaving water that behaves hypotonically and shifts into cells rather than staying in the vasculature where volume is needed.

options.text: It raises blood glucose, which is the only reason it is avoided in trauma
options.rationale: Dextrose does raise serum glucose, and that matters in some patients. The absolute word 'only' also signals a wrong option, because it rules out the actual mechanism.

questions.takeaway: A solution's tonicity can change once it is in the body. D5W is the standing example, which is why it appears on the isotonic list and is still not a volume expander.

questions.stem: A patient has lost an estimated 1200 mL of blood during surgery and has a blood pressure of 88 over 52 with a pulse of 118. While blood is being crossmatched, which solution does the nurse expect to infuse?

options.text: 10% dextrose in water
options.rationale: D10W is hypertonic and is used for hypoglycemia and for expanding intravascular volume. It also carries risks of cell dehydration and hypernatremia that are unnecessary when an isotonic fluid will do the job.

options.text: 0.45% sodium chloride
options.rationale: Half normal saline is hypotonic, so most of the infused water leaves the vasculature and enters cells. A fluid that moves water out of that space is the opposite of what is needed.

options.text: 3% sodium chloride
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline does expand intravascular volume by pulling water out of cells, and it is reserved for severe hyponatremia and cerebral edema. Using it here treats the volume at the cost of dehydrating cells for no reason.

options.text: Lactated Ringer's
options.rationale: Lactated Ringer's is isotonic at 273 mOsm/L, so infused volume stays in the extracellular space and expands circulating volume without shifting water into or out of cells. Volume expansion and hemorrhage resuscitation are the listed uses for isotonic fluids.

questions.takeaway: Hemorrhage empties the vascular compartment, so the fluid that fixes it is the one that stays there. That is the definition of isotonic.

questions.stem: A nurse is preparing to transfuse a unit of packed red blood cells. Which actions are required before the infusion begins? Select all that apply.

options.text: Warm the unit to room temperature on the counter for 30 minutes
options.rationale: Packed red cells are stored between 1 and 6 degrees Celsius and must be infused within 4 hours of issue. Blood warming, when indicated, is done with a dedicated device.

options.text: Have two licensed nurses independently verify the product label against the identification band, ABO and Rh type, unit number, and expiration date
options.rationale: Independent double verification means two qualified people check separately and both sign. Incompatible transfusion is a sentinel event, and this check is what prevents it.

options.text: Establish or confirm an 18 to 20 gauge intravenous access
options.rationale: Gauge describes lumen width, and a wider lumen allows red cells through without excessive resistance. Eighteen to twenty gauge is the stated requirement for blood, and 18 gauge is preferred for blood products specifically.

options.text: Record a full set of baseline vital signs
options.rationale: Baseline vital signs are the values recorded before the infusion starts. Temperature, pulse, respirations, blood pressure, and oxygen saturation are recorded before the unit is started, rechecked at 15 minutes, then every 30 to 60 minutes.

options.text: Confirm that signed informed consent is on file
options.rationale: Informed consent is the patient's documented agreement after being told purpose, benefits, risks, and alternatives. Before the product is retrieved from the blood bank, because the unit's clock and cold chain start the moment it leaves.

options.text: Prime the administration set with 5% dextrose in water
options.rationale: Priming fills the tubing with fluid before connecting it. Dextrose causes red cells to clump and hemolyze, so this action would damage the product being given.

questions.takeaway: The pre-transfusion checks all exist to prevent one event: giving the wrong blood to the wrong patient. Consent, two-nurse verification, adequate access, and baseline vitals.

questions.stem: Two nurses are verifying a unit of blood at the bedside. One nurse reads aloud from the blood bank record while the other listens and agrees. Which statement about this process is correct?

options.text: The process is incorrect, because each nurse must verify the information independently
options.rationale: Independent verification means each nurse checks the source documents and the patient separately and then compares conclusions. The second set of eyes exists to catch the first nurse's error, and it cannot do that if it never looks.

options.text: The verification is complete once both nurses sign the transfusion record
options.rationale: Signing documents that verification occurred. The signature records the process; it does not substitute for it, and both nurses signing a flawed check simply records the flaw twice.

options.text: The process is acceptable as long as one of the two nurses is the nurse who will start the infusion
options.rationale: Which nurse hangs the unit does not change how the check was performed. This adds a true-sounding condition that is irrelevant to the flaw.

options.text: The process is acceptable if the patient states their own name and date of birth
options.rationale: Patient participation in identification is genuinely good practice and confirms one element. Those are the other required elements, and they are checked against documents rather than against the patient's memory.

questions.takeaway: Two-nurse verification means two independent checks, not one check with a witness. The second nurse exists to catch what the first missed.

questions.stem: A unit of packed red blood cells was started 10 minutes ago. The nurse is planning the monitoring schedule for this transfusion. When does the nurse plan the first reassessment of vital signs after initiation?

options.text: At 30 minutes after the start
options.rationale: Every 30 to 60 minutes is the correct interval for the remainder of the transfusion. This is the right number in the wrong position, which makes it the closest wrong answer.

options.text: At 15 minutes after the start
options.rationale: Reassessment at 15 minutes is the scheduled early check after a baseline set. After it, vital signs are taken every 30 to 60 minutes and again at completion.

options.text: At 60 minutes after the start
options.rationale: Sixty minutes is the outer limit of the ongoing interval once the transfusion is established. A substantial part of the unit, which is precisely what the early check is designed to avoid.

options.text: At the halfway point of the unit
options.rationale: Monitoring is scheduled by clock time rather than by volume infused. Rates vary between patients, so a volume-based schedule would place the check at unpredictable times.

questions.takeaway: Baseline, then 15 minutes, then every 30 to 60 minutes, then completion. The 15-minute check exists because early reactions happen in the first small volume.

questions.stem: A patient receiving lactated Ringer's through the only IV site is scheduled for a transfusion. Which action does the nurse take before hanging the blood?

options.text: Flush the existing line with lactated Ringer's and connect the blood to the same tubing
options.rationale: Lactated Ringer's contains calcium. Flushing with it leaves the incompatible fluid in contact with the product.

options.text: Add 5% dextrose in water to the line to keep it open during the transfusion
options.rationale: Dextrose causes red cells to clump and hemolyze on contact. Only 0.9% sodium chloride may contact blood products.

options.text: Change the solution to 0.9% sodium chloride with new tubing before connecting the blood
options.rationale: Normal saline is the only solution permitted with blood products, and new tubing ensures no residual incompatible fluid remains. Isotonic saline is also what flushes before and after the unit.

options.text: Run the blood alongside the lactated Ringer's through a Y connector
options.rationale: A Y connector allows two solutions to meet before entering the vein. The incompatibility is with the blood itself, not with the bag it hangs beside.

questions.takeaway: Only 0.9% sodium chloride touches blood. Dextrose hemolyzes red cells and the calcium in lactated Ringer's clots them.

questions.stem: A patient needs two units of packed red blood cells. The existing peripheral access is a 24 gauge catheter in the dorsal hand. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Use the existing 24 gauge catheter and infuse each unit slowly over 6 hours
options.rationale: Slowing an infusion reduces resistance. This option breaks a second rule to work around the first.

options.text: Use the existing 24 gauge catheter with a pressure bag to overcome the resistance
options.rationale: A pressure bag forces fluid through at a higher driving pressure. Hemolysis, which destroys the product being given and releases its contents into the patient.

options.text: Establish new access with a 22 gauge catheter in the dorsal hand
options.rationale: Twenty-two gauge is a small-bore size recommended for pediatric, elderly, and fragile veins. Dorsal hand veins are also the sites to avoid in older patients and are a poor choice for a viscous product.

options.text: Establish new access with an 18 gauge catheter in a forearm vein
options.rationale: Gauge describes lumen width, and smaller numbers mean wider lumens. A 24 gauge catheter is a small-bore size intended for fragile veins and maintenance fluids.

questions.takeaway: Blood needs 18 to 20 gauge access, with 18 gauge preferred. Working around an inadequate catheter with time or pressure breaks a different rule each time.

questions.stem: A patient scheduled for long-term antibiotic therapy had a left mastectomy with axillary node dissection two years ago and has an arteriovenous fistula in the right forearm for dialysis. Where does the nurse plan vascular access?

options.text: Consultation for a central vascular access device
options.rationale: When both upper extremities are contraindicated and the therapy is long-term, the peripheral options are exhausted rather than merely inconvenient. With a mastectomy limb on one side and a fistula limb on the other, central access is the plan rather than a fallback.

options.text: The right forearm, distal to the fistula
options.rationale: An arteriovenous fistula is a surgical connection between an artery and a vein created for dialysis access. The entire extremity with a fistula is avoided, because that limb's circulation is dedicated to dialysis and cannulation threatens it.

options.text: The left forearm, using the most distal appropriate vein
options.rationale: The affected limb after mastectomy with node dissection has altered lymphatic drainage. The whole limb is avoided, and choosing distal within it applies a correct rule to a site that was already excluded.

options.text: The left external jugular vein
options.rationale: The external jugular is used peripherally in emergencies. It also does not address the underlying problem, which is that this patient needs durable access.

questions.takeaway: Contraindicated sites are contraindicated for the whole limb. When both arms are excluded and therapy is long, central access is the plan rather than the last resort.

questions.stem: A nurse has scrubbed the insertion site with chlorhexidine using friction for 30 seconds. Which action next would require the nurse to repeat the skin preparation?

options.text: Waiting for the antiseptic to dry completely before inserting the catheter
options.rationale: Complete air drying is what allows the antiseptic to exert its full antimicrobial effect. This is the required step, not an error.

options.text: Palpating the vein once more to confirm its position before inserting
options.rationale: Repalpation means touching the cleansed skin with an unsterile finger. Vein position is confirmed before the prep, not after.

options.text: Applying the tourniquet above the site before cleansing
options.rationale: The tourniquet distends the vein to make it visible and palpable. Before, which is the correct order and does not touch the prepared skin.

options.text: Choosing a 20 gauge catheter for the planned infusion
options.rationale: Twenty gauge is the standard adult size, suitable for most medications and fluids. This is a reasonable decision about a different part of the procedure.

questions.takeaway: The prep is only as good as what happens after it. Drying completely and not touching the site are the two steps that preserve the work the scrub did.

questions.stem: A patient has a midline catheter placed for a 10-day course of intravenous antibiotics. Which new prescription does the nurse question?

options.text: Cefazolin 1 g intravenously every 8 hours
options.rationale: An antibiotic is a non-vesicant medication with an osmolarity well within peripheral limits. Antibiotics, analgesics, and hydration therapy are the listed indications.

options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride at 75 mL/hr
options.rationale: Normal saline is isotonic at 308 mOsm/L. Yes, it is one of the named indications.

options.text: Parenteral nutrition at 60 mL/hr
options.rationale: Parenteral nutrition is a highly concentrated solution of dextrose, amino acids, lipids, vitamins, and trace elements. Parenteral nutrition is explicitly excluded from midline use and requires central access, because its osmolarity far exceeds the peripheral limit and would damage the vein.

options.text: Morphine sulfate 2 mg intravenously every 4 hours as needed
options.rationale: Morphine is an analgesic and is not a vesicant. Analgesics are listed among the appropriate therapies.

questions.takeaway: A midline is a long peripheral catheter, not a central line. Its tip ends below the axilla, so it obeys peripheral rules no matter how far up the arm it was inserted.

questions.stem: A peripherally inserted central catheter has just been placed in a patient's right basilic vein. The catheter flushes easily and there is good blood return. Which action does the nurse take before starting the prescribed infusion?

options.text: Measure the external catheter length and compare it with the insertion record
options.rationale: Measuring the external segment detects migration over time by comparison with a baseline. There is no prior measurement, and length does not confirm position inside the chest.

options.text: Confirm placement by the presence of brisk blood return on aspiration
options.rationale: Blood return shows the lumen sits within a vessel and is not occluded. A catheter with its tip in a vein short of the superior vena cava still yields blood return, and those positions carry higher thrombosis rates.

options.text: Begin the infusion at a reduced rate and observe the site for 30 minutes
options.rationale: Starting slowly and observing is a reasonable precaution with peripheral infusions. It begins the therapy before the required confirmation and puts the patient at risk of an infusion into the wrong location.

options.text: Obtain chest radiography to confirm tip placement
options.rationale: Tip confirmation establishes that the catheter ends where it is supposed to, in the lower superior vena cava. A catheter can be patent and still be malpositioned, which is why x-ray confirmation of tip placement is required before use rather than optional.

questions.takeaway: Patency and position are different questions. A PICC can flush, draw back, and still be in the wrong place, which is why radiographic confirmation is required before first use.

questions.stem: A patient is being discharged with a peripherally inserted central catheter in the left arm. Which statement by the patient indicates a correct understanding of the teaching?

options.text: I will have my blood pressure taken in my right arm from now on
options.rationale: Blood pressure measurement compresses the limb under the cuff. Blood pressure cuffs and venipuncture are both avoided on the PICC arm, so moving them to the other side is the correct understanding.

options.text: I can take a bath as long as I change the dressing afterward
options.rationale: Submerging the arm puts the exit site under water regardless of what follows. Baths and swimming are avoided entirely, and showering is done with a waterproof cover over the site.

options.text: If the line feels blocked I should push a little harder on the syringe to clear it
options.rationale: Resistance during flushing means something is obstructing the lumen. The instruction is to stop and not use the line if resistance is felt.

options.text: I should change the dressing whenever I remember, about once a month
options.rationale: The dressing keeps the exit site clean, dry, and intact. A monthly interval leaves the site unprotected for weeks, and monthly flushing belongs to an implanted port rather than a PICC.

questions.takeaway: The PICC arm is off limits for blood pressure cuffs and venipuncture, and the site stays dry. Resistance on flushing is a stop signal, not something to push through.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses an intravenous site and finds the surrounding skin is cool and pale with moderate swelling. The drip rate has slowed and no blood return is obtained. Which complication has occurred?

options.text: Phlebitis
options.rationale: Phlebitis is inflammation of the vein wall itself, producing pain, redness, warmth, a streak along the vein, and a palpable cord. Inflammation raises local temperature, so a cool site points away from phlebitis even though both complications look alarming.

options.text: Infiltration
options.rationale: Infiltration is IV fluid leaking out of the vein into the surrounding tissue. Fluid sitting in the interstitium makes the skin cool and pale and produces edema, the catheter is no longer in the vessel so there is no blood return, and the resistance of the tissue slows the drip rate.

options.text: Hematoma
options.rationale: A hematoma is blood leaking into tissue at the insertion site, producing bruising, swelling, and tenderness. Swelling is shared between the two, which is what makes this worth checking rather than dismissing.

options.text: Thrombosis
options.rationale: Thrombosis is a clot forming in or around the catheter, producing a swollen, painful limb and a decreased flow rate. A clot slows flow, and it does not push fluid into the tissue.

questions.takeaway: Cool and pale means fluid has left the vein. Warm and red with a cord means the vein wall is inflamed. Both begin with stopping the infusion and removing the catheter.

questions.stem: While a nurse is changing the injection cap on a patient's central venous catheter, the patient suddenly reports chest pain and severe shortness of breath. The blood pressure falls to 84 over 48 and a churning murmur is audible over the precordium. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Position the patient in left lateral Trendelenburg
options.rationale: Left lateral Trendelenburg traps air in the right atrium away from the pulmonary outflow tract so it cannot be pumped into the lungs. It manages the air already inside while clamping prevents more.

options.text: Administer 100 percent oxygen by nonrebreather mask
options.rationale: High-flow oxygen improves saturation and helps the trapped air be reabsorbed. It is part of the response and it does not stop air from entering.

options.text: Clamp the catheter tubing
options.rationale: Clamping closes the pathway between room air and the venous system. Stopping the source is the first action because every additional second adds volume to the embolus, and the remaining steps treat what has already entered.

options.text: Activate the rapid response team
options.rationale: A rapid response brings additional expertise to the bedside. Calling is essential and it is not the first action when a one-second intervention stops the cause.

questions.takeaway: Sudden dyspnea, chest pain, hypotension, and a mill-wheel murmur during line manipulation is air embolism. Clamp, position in left lateral Trendelenburg, call rapid response, and give 100 percent oxygen.

questions.stem: For each patient situation, indicate the vascular access device the nurse anticipates.

rows.text: Needs a single dose of intravenous antiemetic in the emergency department and is expected to go home the same day
rows.rationale: A short peripheral catheter is the standard device for short-term therapy with isotonic or mildly hypertonic solutions. Nothing about this situation calls for a longer or deeper device.

rows.text: Needs 10 days of intravenous antibiotics and has poor forearm veins that will not sustain repeated short catheters
rows.rationale: A midline is 3 to 8 inches, placed in the upper arm with its tip below the axilla, and dwells up to 4 weeks. Midlines are indicated for antibiotics, analgesics, and hydration.

rows.text: Requires parenteral nutrition at home for the next several weeks after bowel surgery
rows.rationale: Parenteral nutrition is highly concentrated and requires a tip in central circulation. A PICC, whose tip sits in the lower superior vena cava and which is specifically indicated for parenteral nutrition, vesicants, and irritating medications.

rows.text: Will receive chemotherapy every three weeks for the next year and wants to continue swimming between cycles
rows.rationale: An implanted port is a subcutaneous reservoir with no external catheter, accessed with a non-coring needle and flushed monthly when not in use. It also carries the lowest infection risk of the central devices.

rows.text: Has end-stage kidney disease and needs immediate access for treatment while a fistula matures
rows.rationale: A hemodialysis catheter is large bore at 11 to 14 French to allow the rapid blood withdrawal and return that dialysis requires. It is dedicated to dialysis, never used for routine infusion or blood draws, and managed by dialysis-trained staff.

rows.text: Needs a continuous vasopressor infusion titrated in the intensive care unit and already has a central catheter in the internal jugular vein
rows.rationale: This row is the trap in the set. A PICC provides central access for weeks to months with far lower infection risk than a nontunneled catheter, which carries the highest infection risk of the central devices and is intended for days to weeks.

questions.takeaway: Device selection runs on four criteria: therapy duration, solution osmolarity, vein condition, and patient diagnosis and preference. Duration sets the family of devices and the solution decides whether the tip must be central.

questions.nursesNote: 1400: Patient admitted for dehydration after three days of poor oral intake. Prescribed 0.9% sodium chloride at 150 mL per hour. Access is a 22 gauge catheter in the left forearm, placed on the first attempt. 1600: Patient is oriented to person, place, and time and reports feeling steadier. Lungs clear to auscultation bilaterally. Heart rate 84, blood pressure 128 over 76, respirations 16, oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air. Urine output 60 mL over the past hour. 1900: Patient asks the same question about the time three times in ten minutes. Respirations 26 and shallow. Fine crackles audible at both lung bases. Oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air. Heart rate 104. Blood pressure 152 over 88. Skin at the IV site is intact with good blood return and no redness.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings at 1900 that require the nurse to intervene.

segments.text: Patient asks the same question about the time three times in ten minutes
segments.rationale: New confusion is a change in mental status from a documented baseline. Confusion is one of the three findings to assess frequently in an older adult receiving fluids, and it is the one most often attributed to age or to the hospital instead of to the volume being infused.

segments.text: Respirations 26 and shallow
segments.rationale: Tachypnea is a respiratory rate above normal. Dyspnea is a listed sign of fluid overload, and rapid shallow breathing is how it presents before the patient reports it.

segments.text: Fine crackles audible at both lung bases
segments.rationale: Crackles are the sound of fluid in the small airways. Crackles are the third of the three findings named for frequent assessment in this population, and new bibasilar crackles during an infusion is pulmonary edema until proven otherwise.

segments.text: Oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air
segments.rationale: Oxygen saturation measures how much hemoglobin is carrying oxygen. Fluid in the alveoli interferes with gas exchange, which is the mechanism connecting this value to the crackles.

segments.text: Heart rate 104
segments.rationale: Tachycardia is a heart rate above 100. It supports the assessment and does not independently demand action.

segments.text: Blood pressure 152 over 88
segments.rationale: A rising blood pressure can accompany volume expansion. It is elevated and not dangerous, and the note gives no prior hypertension history to compare it against.

segments.text: Skin at the IV site is intact with good blood return and no redness
segments.rationale: Blood return and intact skin indicate the catheter is within the vessel and the site is uninflamed. Infiltration and phlebitis are both excluded, which is what tells you the problem is systemic rather than local.

segments.text: Urine output 60 mL over the past hour
segments.rationale: Urine output reflects renal perfusion and fluid handling. This value was recorded at 1600 and is not a 1900 finding.

questions.takeaway: Confusion, dyspnea, and crackles are one finding wearing three coats in an older patient receiving fluids. All three are early fluid overload, and confusion is the one that gets blamed on something else.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A patient receiving intravenous vancomycin through a forearm catheter reports burning at the site. The nurse finds redness extending along the line of the vein, warmth, and a firm cord that can be palpated for about half an inch. There is blood return and no swelling.

These findings indicate [[1]].

The nurse's first action is to [[2]].

The most likely cause in this patient is [[3]].

options.text: infiltration
options.rationale: Infiltration is fluid leaking into surrounding tissue, producing cool pale skin, edema, a slowed drip, and no blood return. Blood return is present and there is no swelling, so the fluid has not left the vein.

options.text: phlebitis
options.rationale: Phlebitis is inflammation of the vein wall. Redness along the vein, warmth, and a palpable cord are the defining signs, and the presence of blood return with no swelling tells you the catheter is still in the vessel.

options.text: a hematoma
options.rationale: A hematoma is blood collecting in tissue at the insertion site, producing bruising, swelling, and tenderness. Redness, and there is no swelling.

options.text: a catheter-related bloodstream infection
options.rationale: A CRBSI is a systemic infection with fever, chills, hypotension, and altered mental status and no other identifiable source. No, everything described is local to the site and the vein.

options.text: apply a cold compress and continue the infusion
options.rationale: Cold reduces local blood flow and can ease discomfort. No, and a warm moist compress rather than cold is what the intervention for phlebitis specifies.

options.text: flush the catheter with normal saline to test patency
options.rationale: Flushing checks whether the lumen is open. Blood return is already present, so flushing adds volume to an inflamed vein and delays removal.

options.text: stop the infusion and remove the catheter
options.rationale: Stopping ends the exposure and removing the catheter takes out the object inflaming the vein. Nothing useful happens while the catheter stays in an inflamed vein.

options.text: slow the infusion and reassess in one hour
options.rationale: Slowing reduces the rate at which an irritating drug reaches the vein. The intervention for phlebitis is to stop, not to moderate.

options.text: mechanical irritation from catheter movement
options.rationale: Mechanical phlebitis results from the catheter moving within the vein, usually from an oversized catheter or an unsecured one at a point of flexion. This is a real type of phlebitis and it is not what this stem describes.

options.text: bacterial contamination from poor aseptic technique
options.rationale: Bacterial phlebitis follows a break in asepsis and tends to appear with systemic signs or purulent drainage at grade 4. It is one of the three types and the stem gives no evidence for it.

options.text: an allergic reaction to the medication
options.rationale: An allergic reaction produces urticaria, itching, bronchospasm, or hypotension and is systemic rather than confined to one vein. Along the vein, which is inflammation rather than hypersensitivity.

options.text: chemical irritation from the infused medication
options.rationale: Chemical phlebitis is inflammation caused by an irritating solution. The drug named in the stem is the evidence that selects this type.

questions.takeaway: Phlebitis has three types and they are separated by the history, not by the appearance. Mechanical is about the catheter, chemical is about the solution, bacterial is about technique.

questions.scenario: A patient with a nontunneled central venous catheter in the subclavian vein has been receiving intravenous antibiotics for four days. Over the past two hours the patient has become confused and is shaking with chills. Temperature is 39.1 C, heart rate 126, blood pressure 86 over 48, respirations 24, oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. The catheter exit site is clean and dry with no redness or drainage. The lungs are clear, the urine is clear and pale, and the abdomen is soft and nontender. The patient has no cough, no wound, and no other invasive devices.
questions.stem: Select 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 problem they address, and 2 parameters to evaluate.

options.text: Remove the dressing and repalpate the site to check for tenderness
options.rationale: Repalpating a central line site with unsterile fingers contaminates it. This adds risk without adding information.

options.text: Apply a warm compress to the catheter exit site
options.rationale: Warm compresses are used for phlebitis at a peripheral site. This treats a finding that is not present.

options.text: Obtain two sets of blood cultures before antibiotics are changed
options.rationale: Blood cultures identify the organism in the bloodstream and the paired sets help establish whether the catheter is the source. Because once the drug is in, the organism may not grow, and the identification determines the treatment.

options.text: Notify the provider and prepare for possible catheter removal
options.rationale: Removal eliminates the source when the catheter is the origin of the infection. The nontunneled catheter carries the highest infection risk of the central devices and is the only plausible source here.

options.text: Slow the antibiotic infusion and recheck the temperature in one hour
options.rationale: Slowing an infusion is a response to speed shock or to an infusion reaction. Delaying an hour in a hypotensive, febrile patient forfeits the time in which cultures and treatment matter most.

options.text: Speed shock
options.rationale: Speed shock is a drug reaching a toxic concentration because it entered too quickly, producing flushing, headache, chest tightness, and shock. Fever and rigors, which speed shock does not cause.

options.text: Catheter thrombosis
options.rationale: Thrombosis is a clot in or around the catheter, producing a swollen painful limb and a decreased flow rate. It also does not produce fever with rigors.

options.text: Air embolism
options.rationale: Air embolism follows air entering the venous system, producing sudden dyspnea, chest pain, a mill-wheel murmur, and hypotension. No, it developed over two hours with fever and chills.

options.text: Catheter-related bloodstream infection
options.rationale: A CRBSI is a bloodstream infection caused by the catheter, presenting with fever, chills, hypotension, and altered mental status and no other identifiable source. Clear lungs, clear urine, soft abdomen, no cough, no wound, and no other devices leave the four-day central line as the source.

options.text: Appearance of the catheter exit site over the next 24 hours
options.rationale: Exit site appearance detects local infection. A bloodstream infection can occur with a normal-looking site, so watching it measures the wrong thing.

options.text: Blood pressure response to treatment
options.rationale: Blood pressure reflects perfusion, and 86 over 48 is the finding that makes this urgent rather than merely concerning. A rising pressure as the systemic response is controlled.

options.text: Whether the patient reports pain at the insertion site
options.rationale: Site pain is a local symptom. No, and the stem already establishes the site is unremarkable.

options.text: Temperature trend over the next several hours
options.rationale: Temperature reflects the systemic inflammatory response to the infection. Directly, and a falling temperature after cultures and treatment is the expected response.

options.text: Volume of antibiotic infused per hour
options.rationale: Infusion volume records what was delivered. No, it measures the nurse's task completion.

questions.takeaway: A catheter-related bloodstream infection is diagnosed partly by exclusion, and a clean exit site does not rule it out. Dwell time is a primary risk factor, which is why line necessity is reviewed daily.

questions.stem: A patient is receiving 3% sodium chloride. Which assessments does the nurse prioritize?

options.text: Serum glucose and urine ketones
options.rationale: Relevant to dextrose-containing fluids and ketoacidosis, not to hypertonic saline.

options.text: Platelet count and coagulation studies
options.rationale: Not affected by sodium concentration.

options.text: Liver enzymes and serum albumin
options.rationale: Not the parameters altered by hypertonic saline.

options.text: Serum sodium, neurological status, and fluid balance
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline pulls water out of cells and raises sodium. Those three are the stated monitoring priorities.

questions.takeaway: Hypertonic solutions risk cell dehydration, hypernatremia, and circulatory overload.

questions.stem: A patient becomes flushed and reports a pounding headache and chest tightness moments after an intravenous medication is given. Which complication does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Speed shock
options.rationale: A drug reaching a toxic concentration because it entered too quickly. Flushing, headache, chest tightness, and shock are the picture.

options.text: Air embolism
options.rationale: Produces sudden dyspnea, chest pain, a mill-wheel murmur, and hypotension, usually during line manipulation.

options.text: Infiltration
options.rationale: A local problem producing cool, pale, swollen tissue and no blood return.

options.text: Phlebitis
options.rationale: Inflammation of the vein wall producing redness, warmth, and a palpable cord over time.

questions.takeaway: Prevent speed shock with an infusion pump, verified rates, and never bolusing concentrated drugs.

questions.stem: Which nursing action most directly reduces the risk of a central line infection over time?

options.text: Changing the transparent dressing every 7 days
options.rationale: Necessary maintenance, and it does not shorten how long the line stays in.

options.text: Reviewing daily whether the catheter is still necessary and removing it promptly
options.rationale: Dwell time is a primary risk factor. Every extra day raises risk, so removal is the strongest lever.

options.text: Flushing each lumen after every medication
options.rationale: Maintains patency rather than preventing infection.

options.text: Labeling the tubing with the date it was hung
options.rationale: Supports timely tubing changes but does not address dwell time.

questions.takeaway: The line that is no longer needed is the one that infects the patient.

questions.stem: Before accessing a needleless connector on a central line, the nurse scrubs the hub. Which technique is correct?

options.text: A quick wipe with an alcohol pad immediately before access
options.rationale: Too brief to reduce organisms on the surface.

options.text: Chlorhexidine applied and wiped dry with gauze
options.rationale: Wiping removes the antiseptic before it has acted.

options.text: Alcohol pad with friction for at least 15 seconds, every time
options.rationale: Fifteen seconds of friction is the stated standard and it applies to every access, not just the first.

options.text: Scrubbing only when the connector appears soiled
options.rationale: A clean-looking hub is still colonized. The scrub is unconditional.

questions.takeaway: Scrub the hub at least 15 seconds, every access.

questions.stem: A nurse is preparing to access an implanted port. Which equipment is required?

options.text: A standard hypodermic needle and clean gloves
options.rationale: A standard bevel cuts a plug out of the septum and destroys it over time.

options.text: A butterfly needle with a transparent dressing
options.rationale: Winged needles are for single-dose injections and blood draws, not port access.

options.text: A blunt cannula through the needleless connector
options.rationale: There is no external connector on a port. The skin and septum must be punctured.

options.text: A non-coring Huber needle and a mask using aseptic technique
options.rationale: The deflected tip slices the septum instead of coring it out, preserving the septum for repeated access.

questions.takeaway: Ports are accessed only by trained staff, with a non-coring needle, a mask, and aseptic technique.

questions.stem: A patient with a tunneled hemodialysis catheter needs intravenous antibiotics. The peripheral veins are difficult. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Request an order for alternate vascular access
options.rationale: The dialysis catheter is critical to managing kidney failure and is reserved. Another device is obtained for the antibiotics.

options.text: Use the dialysis catheter since it is already in place
options.rationale: It is dedicated to dialysis and is not used for routine infusion or blood draws.

options.text: Use the unused lumen of the dialysis catheter only
options.rationale: Both lumens are reserved. Having a spare does not change the restriction.

options.text: Flush the dialysis catheter with saline and then infuse
options.rationale: Also uses the reserved catheter, and it discards the heparin lock that maintains it.

questions.takeaway: Hemodialysis catheters are dialysis only, managed by dialysis-trained staff, except in an emergency.

questions.stem: Which patient is the best candidate for hypodermoclysis?

options.text: A patient in hypovolemic shock after trauma
options.rationale: Clysis is explicitly avoided in severe dehydration and shock. It is too slow.

options.text: An older patient with mild dehydration receiving palliative care
options.rationale: Slow, steady, short-term rehydration in an elderly or palliative patient is the stated indication.

options.text: A patient needing rapid transfusion of packed red blood cells
options.rationale: Blood products require vascular access, not subcutaneous tissue.

options.text: A patient requiring continuous vasopressor infusion
options.rationale: Vasopressors are vesicants requiring central venous access.

questions.takeaway: Hypodermoclysis is slow rehydration, roughly 1 mL per minute, never resuscitation.

questions.stem: An intraosseous needle was placed in a patient's proximal tibia during a cardiac arrest. The patient now has return of circulation and a peripheral intravenous line has been established. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Leave the intraosseous needle in place for 72 hours as a backup
options.rationale: Exceeds the 24-hour limit and raises the risk of osteomyelitis.

options.text: Continue using the intraosseous route for all medications
options.rationale: Continuing an unnecessary bone access adds infection risk with no benefit.

options.text: Remove the intraosseous needle now that vascular access is available
options.rationale: Intraosseous access is for the immediate resuscitation period only, and it is discontinued as soon as it is no longer needed.

options.text: Flush the intraosseous needle every 8 hours to keep it patent
options.rationale: Maintains a device that should be removed.

questions.takeaway: Intraosseous access is limited to 24 hours and removed as soon as it is no longer needed.

questions.stem: A patient has a serum potassium of 2.9 mEq/L. Urine output has been 15 mL per hour for the past four hours and the creatinine is rising. The provider orders potassium chloride 20 mEq in 100 mL over one hour. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Administer the dose on a pump as ordered, since the potassium is low
options.rationale: The rate and the pump are correct, and the kidney data make the order itself unsafe. A low value does not override the route out.

options.text: Give half the ordered dose and recheck the potassium in two hours
options.rationale: Changing a dose independently is outside nursing scope, and half a dose still has no way to leave the body.

options.text: Administer the dose more slowly over two hours
options.rationale: Slowing reduces the peak and does nothing about accumulation in a patient who is not excreting.

options.text: Hold the dose and contact the provider about the urine output
options.rationale: Potassium is excreted by the kidney. Output of 15 mL per hour with a rising creatinine means the patient cannot clear it, and giving potassium to failing kidneys converts a low value into a dangerous one.

questions.takeaway: Never push, never undiluted, never into a hanging bag, always on a pump, and confirm urine output first.

questions.stem: A patient with kidney failure has a potassium of 6.9 mEq/L. The monitor shows tall peaked T waves and a QRS that has widened since the previous strip. The patient is alert with a blood pressure of 104/62. Which order does the nurse anticipate first?

options.text: Intravenous calcium gluconate
options.rationale: Calcium stabilizes the myocardium so the widening QRS does not progress to arrest. It does not lower the potassium, and that is the point: it buys time while the measures that actually remove potassium take effect.

options.text: Intravenous insulin with dextrose
options.rationale: Shifts potassium into cells and lowers the serum value within about 15 to 30 minutes. It is part of the treatment and it does not protect the heart in the interval before it works.

options.text: Oral potassium-binding agent
options.rationale: Removes potassium from the body through the gut, which is the slowest of the three actions. Correct and not first when the QRS is already widening.

options.text: Arrangement for urgent hemodialysis
options.rationale: Definitively removes potassium and takes time to arrange and initiate. The heart needs protecting before then.

questions.takeaway: Hyperkalemia treatment runs in three moves: stabilize the heart, shift potassium into cells, then remove it from the body.

questions.stem: Ten hours after a total thyroidectomy a patient reports tingling of the fingers and around the mouth. The voice sounds hoarse and the patient has begun clearing the throat repeatedly. Chvostek sign is positive. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Test for Trousseau sign with a blood pressure cuff
options.rationale: It would confirm the same hyperexcitability already demonstrated by Chvostek, and inflating a cuff for three minutes spends time while airway symptoms are developing.

options.text: Ensure emergency airway equipment is at the bedside and notify the provider
options.rationale: A positive Chvostek sign with perioral tingling after thyroid surgery indicates hypocalcemia, and hoarseness with throat clearing raises the concern for laryngospasm. Airway comes before the calcium.

options.text: Draw a serum calcium and await the result
options.rationale: The laboratory value will confirm what the findings already say. Waiting on it delays the airway preparation.

options.text: Offer oral calcium with vitamin D from the medication record
options.rationale: Replacement is the treatment and takes time to act. Nothing is given by mouth to a patient whose airway may be about to close.

questions.takeaway: Cheek for Chvostek, cuff for Trousseau. Both mean low calcium or magnesium, and laryngospasm is what turns a lab value into an emergency.

questions.stem: A patient is receiving a continuous magnesium sulfate infusion. Over the past hour the patellar reflexes have become difficult to elicit, respirations have fallen from 18 to 11 per minute, and urine output was 20 mL in the last hour. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Administer calcium gluconate
options.rationale: Calcium gluconate is the antidote and will be given. It is the second action, because magnesium continues to enter while it is drawn up.

options.text: Notify the provider of the reflex and respiratory changes
options.rationale: Essential and immediately after stopping the drug. Reporting while the infusion runs lets the level keep climbing.

options.text: Stop the infusion
options.rationale: Loss of reflexes followed by respiratory depression is magnesium excess, and the falling urine output means the patient is not clearing it. Stopping ends the source, and it is the one action that takes seconds.

options.text: Increase the intravenous fluid rate to promote excretion
options.rationale: Does not address the source and adds volume to a patient whose output has fallen to 20 mL per hour.

questions.takeaway: Reflexes disappear before breathing does, which is the warning. Stop the drug, then give calcium gluconate.

questions.stem: A patient who has had vomiting and diarrhea for three days is admitted. Which findings support fluid volume deficit? Select all that apply.

options.text: Blood pressure falls from 124/78 supine to 98/60 on sitting
options.rationale: There is not enough circulating volume to maintain pressure against a position change, which is orthostatic hypotension.

options.text: Urine output of 18 mL per hour with a specific gravity of 1.032
options.rationale: Low output with highly concentrated urine. The kidney is holding on to every available drop of water.

options.text: Hematocrit of 54 percent
options.rationale: Hemoconcentration. Losing plasma water without losing red cells raises the proportion that red cells occupy.

options.text: Weight down 2.5 kg since admission three days ago
options.rationale: About 2.5 liters. Daily weight is the most sensitive fluid measure available.

options.text: Jugular veins visible at 45 degrees with a bounding radial pulse
options.rationale: Distended neck veins and a bounding pulse are signs of excess volume, not deficit.

options.text: Crackles audible at both lung bases
options.rationale: Fluid in the alveoli indicates overload. A patient who is dry does not develop crackles from the deficit.

questions.takeaway: Deficit is dry, flat, and concentrated. Excess is wet, distended, and dilute. Read the labs with the exam.

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure has a recorded 24-hour intake of 1400 mL and output of 1500 mL, which the nurse notes as a slightly negative balance. The morning weight is up 1.6 kg from yesterday. Which conclusion does the nurse draw?

options.text: The intake and output record is accurate and the scale should be recalibrated
options.rationale: A 1.6 kg overnight change is well outside scale error, and the records are the less reliable of the two.

options.text: The gain represents improved nutritional status
options.rationale: Nutritional gain accrues over weeks. It does not appear overnight in a patient with heart failure.

options.text: Both measures are normal daily variation and need no action
options.rationale: In a patient with heart failure, 1.6 kg overnight is a finding to act on regardless of what the balance sheet says.

options.text: The weight is more reliable, and the patient has retained roughly 1.6 liters
options.rationale: One kilogram is about one liter. Intake and output records miss insensible losses, unmeasured intake, and inconsistent charting, so a weight that disagrees with them is the measure to trust.

questions.takeaway: When the flowsheet and the scale disagree, believe the scale. Same time, same scale, same clothing.

questions.stem: A nurse is observing a new graduate prepare to transfuse platelets. Which action requires the nurse to intervene?

options.text: The graduate retrieves the platelets and places them in the unit refrigerator while gathering supplies
options.rationale: Platelets are stored at room temperature with agitation, and refrigeration destroys platelet function. Cold storage preserves red cells and ruins this product.

options.text: The graduate primes the administration set with 0.9% sodium chloride
options.rationale: Normal saline is the only solution permitted to contact any blood product.

options.text: The graduate asks a second licensed nurse to verify the unit independently
options.rationale: Two-nurse verification is required for every blood component, not only for red cells.

options.text: The graduate records a full set of vital signs before starting the infusion
options.rationale: Baseline vital signs are recorded before any transfusion begins and are the comparison for every later reading.

questions.takeaway: Storage tells you what a product is made of. Cold for red cells, room temperature with agitation for platelets, frozen for plasma.

questions.stem: A patient will receive chemotherapy every three weeks for the next year, swims twice weekly, and has had two peripheral lines infiltrate during the first cycle. Which device does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: A peripherally inserted central catheter
options.rationale: Provides the central access chemotherapy requires and has an external catheter with a dressing that must stay dry, which rules out swimming.

options.text: An implanted port
options.rationale: Nothing sits outside the skin, which gives it the lowest infection risk and allows swimming. It suits intermittent therapy over more than a year and is accessed with a non-coring needle when needed.

options.text: A tunneled central venous catheter
options.rationale: Appropriate for frequent long-term therapy and has an external catheter needing daily care. Some patients choose it over a port specifically to avoid needlesticks, and this patient's schedule is intermittent.

options.text: A midline catheter
options.rationale: Peripheral, with the tip below the axilla. Vesicant chemotherapy is excluded from midline use.

questions.takeaway: Match the device to duration, solution, and the patient's life. Intermittent therapy over a year with water exposure points to a port.

questions.stem: A nurse is using the Bedside Mobility Assessment Tool. The patient sits at the side of the bed unassisted for three minutes, reaches across midline, and shakes the nurse's hand. With both feet flat on the floor and the knees below hip level, the patient straightens each knee and points the toes. When asked to rise, the patient cannot lift the buttocks off the bed. Which mobility level does this patient have?

options.text: Level 3, moderate assist
options.rationale: Level 3 is assigned when the patient fails the stand test, which checks lower-extremity strength for standing. The patient passed the first two tests and failed the third, which means there is some lower-extremity strength but not enough to progress toward walking.

options.text: Level 1, total assist
options.rationale: Level 1 is assigned when the patient fails the sit and shake test, which checks trunk strength and seated balance. The first test was passed, so Level 1 is ruled out by the stem.

options.text: Level 2, maximum assist
options.rationale: Level 2 is assigned when the patient fails the stretch and point test, which checks lower-extremity strength and stability. The second test was passed as well.

options.text: Level 4, minimum or standby assist
options.rationale: Level 4 requires passing the walk test, which checks standing balance and gait by having the patient march in place and advance a foot. You cannot skip a failed test to reach a higher level.

questions.takeaway: The tool is a sequence of four tests, and the level is named by the first test the patient cannot complete. Sit and shake, stretch and point, stand, walk.

questions.stem: A patient has completed the sitting and lower-extremity portions of the Bedside Mobility Assessment Tool successfully. Before asking the patient to rise toward standing, which factor does the nurse evaluate?

options.text: Whether an assistive device is available at the bedside
options.rationale: An assistive device is equipment such as a walker or cane that supports weight and balance. Having one ready is sensible and is not the evaluation specified before this test, which makes this the closest wrong answer.

options.text: The patient's cognition, orientation, and whether delirium is present
options.rationale: Delirium is an acute, fluctuating confusion with a physical cause. Standing is the point where the assessment first puts the patient's weight on their own legs, so mental status is checked before it rather than after.

options.text: The patient's grip strength in both hands
options.rationale: Grip strength measures hand and forearm function. Grip was already sampled during the handshake in the first test, and it says nothing about the legs.

options.text: Whether the patient reached across midline during the earlier step
options.rationale: Reaching across midline demonstrates trunk control and seated balance. It is accurate information that has already done its work.

questions.takeaway: Strength and judgment are separate systems and fail separately. A patient whose legs work and whose thinking does not will stand up and go down.

questions.stem: A patient has left-sided weakness after a stroke. The patient can raise the left arm about halfway toward shoulder height and then cannot lift it any further. Which exercise does the nurse use to maintain shoulder mobility?

options.text: Passive range of motion, with the nurse moving the arm through the whole arc
options.rationale: Passive range of motion means someone else moves the joint while the patient's muscle does nothing. Taking over the whole arc wastes the muscle activity the patient still has, and passive work maintains flexibility without building strength.

options.text: Active range of motion, with the patient raising the arm through the full arc unaided
options.rationale: Active range of motion means the patient performs the entire movement alone. The joint would never reach full range, and stiffness would develop in the part that is never used.

options.text: Active-assistive range of motion, with the patient raising the arm as far as possible and the nurse completing the movement
options.rationale: Active-assistive range of motion means the patient moves the joint as far as they can and the nurse supplies the remainder. The muscle works through the portion the patient controls, which preserves strength, and the joint still reaches full range, which preserves flexibility.

options.text: Isometric exercise, with the patient tightening the shoulder muscles without moving the joint
options.rationale: Isometric exercise contracts the muscle without moving the joint. Isometric work builds static strength and joint stability and does nothing for range.

questions.takeaway: Whenever a patient can contribute any part of a movement, they do that part. Active-assistive is the choice that keeps muscle working and still carries the joint through full range.

questions.stem: A patient has a long arm cast after a forearm fracture and will wear it for six weeks. The patient asks how to avoid losing strength in that arm. Which exercise does the nurse teach?

options.text: Move the elbow and wrist through their full range several times daily
options.rationale: Range of motion carries a joint through its arc. Joints above and below a cast are exercised where they are free, and the joints inside it are immobilized on purpose while the bone heals.

options.text: Lift a light hand weight with the casted arm
options.rationale: Lifting a weight through an arc is isotonic exercise, in which the muscle contracts while the joint moves. This is the correct exercise for building dynamic strength and the wrong one for a limb that must stay still.

options.text: Rest the arm completely until the cast is removed
options.rationale: Complete rest means no muscle activity at all. Resting sounds protective and guarantees the outcome the patient asked how to avoid.

options.text: Tighten and release the muscles inside the cast without moving the joints
options.rationale: Isometric exercise contracts the muscle without joint movement. It increases static strength and builds joint stability, and it can be used safely around painful or healing tissue, so the muscle keeps working for the six weeks the joint cannot.

questions.takeaway: Isometric exercise is the answer when a joint must not move. The muscle can still be loaded, so strength and joint stability survive the period of immobilization.

questions.stem: A patient walks the length of the hallway with a nurse. Which findings indicate that the patient exceeded activity tolerance? Select all that apply.

options.text: The patient becomes light-headed and reaches for the handrail
options.rationale: Dizziness is a listed tolerance parameter and it signals that perfusion to the brain has dropped. A patient who needs the handrail to stay upright is at the point where the activity becomes a fall.

options.text: Heart rate remains 118 ten minutes after returning to the chair
options.rationale: Recovery is the last item on the list of things to evaluate and the one most often skipped. A sustained elevation says the patient did more than the cardiovascular system could absorb, even if the walk itself looked acceptable.

options.text: Heart rate rises from 78 to 92 during the walk and returns to 80 within two minutes of sitting
options.rationale: Activity tolerance is judged by the response to activity and by the recovery afterward. This is the body working correctly, not failing.

options.text: Oxygen saturation falls from 96 percent to 87 percent during the walk
options.rationale: Oxygen saturation measures how much of the hemoglobin is carrying oxygen. Oxygenation is one of the listed tolerance parameters, and a drop of nine points into the eighties means demand has outrun the patient's ability to supply it.

options.text: The patient stops twice and says it is hard to catch a breath
options.rationale: Dyspnea is the subjective sense of not getting enough air. Having to stop is the functional version of the same finding.

options.text: Respiratory rate rises from 16 to 20 and settles back to 16 after three minutes
options.rationale: Respiratory rate is one of the tolerance parameters. A modest increase during walking that resolves on sitting is the expected response.

questions.takeaway: Activity tolerance is heart rate, respiratory rate, oxygenation, dyspnea, fatigue, pain, dizziness, and the ability to recover afterward. Rises during exertion are expected; what matters is how large they are and whether they resolve.

questions.stem: A nurse performs a neurovascular assessment on a patient six hours after surgical repair of an ankle fracture. Which finding does the nurse report to the provider immediately?

options.text: Capillary refill of four seconds in the toes with new numbness of the foot, compared with two seconds and normal sensation on the other side
options.rationale: Capillary refill is the time for color to return after pressure on the nail bed, normally under three seconds, and numbness is loss of sensation. Absent or diminished pulses, a cool or pale extremity, new numbness, and sudden loss of movement are all findings to report.

options.text: Moderate swelling at the surgical site
options.rationale: Swelling is fluid accumulating in injured tissue. What would concern you is swelling that is rapid or increasing quickly, and the stem describes neither.

options.text: Bruising visible along the lateral ankle
options.rationale: Bruising is blood that has escaped into the tissue from the injury and the surgery. It is an expected finding after a fracture and its repair.

options.text: Pain rated 5 of 10 that decreases after the ordered analgesic
options.rationale: Pain is one of the neurovascular parameters. This pain responded to the ordered dose, which is the reassuring version of the finding.

questions.takeaway: Neurovascular assessment is color, temperature, capillary refill, pulses, sensation, movement, and pain, and it is always compared side to side. Two abnormal findings in the same limb with a normal opposite side is the pattern that gets reported.

questions.stem: A patient has been immobile in bed for two weeks following a spinal cord injury. The nurse finds that both feet rest with the toes pointed downward and the ankles can no longer be brought to a neutral position. Which complication has developed?

options.text: Bone demineralization
options.rationale: Bone demineralization is the loss of mineral from bone that is not being loaded. It shows on imaging or in calcium studies, not as a joint that will not move.

options.text: Foot drop, which is a plantar flexion contracture
options.rationale: A contracture is the permanent shortening of muscle and tendon that limits joint mobility, and plantar flexion is the toes-pointed position of the ankle. That is foot drop, and it is prevented by maintaining neutral alignment, performing range of motion, and using supportive devices.

options.text: Muscle atrophy
options.rationale: Atrophy is the shrinking of muscle that is not being used. This patient almost certainly has atrophy too, and atrophy does not lock a joint in a fixed position, which is what the stem describes.

options.text: Venous stasis
options.rationale: Venous stasis is blood pooling in the legs because the muscle pump has stopped working. It raises the risk of thrombus formation and presents as swelling or as a clot, not as a rigid ankle.

questions.takeaway: Contractures are permanent shortening, so prevention is the whole intervention. Range of motion, neutral alignment, and supportive devices are scheduled rather than offered when there is time.

questions.stem: A patient is on bed rest after spinal surgery. The nurse hears diminished breath sounds at both lung bases with no adventitious sounds, notes that the patient's cough is weak, and finds that the oxygen saturation has fallen from 97 to 92 percent. The temperature is 36.8 C. Which complication is developing?

options.text: Pneumonia
options.rationale: Pneumonia is infection of the lung tissue. It has not yet.

options.text: Thrombus formation in the legs
options.rationale: A thrombus is a clot forming in a vein where blood has stopped moving. Thrombus is a genuine risk for this patient and is not what these findings describe.

options.text: Atelectasis
options.rationale: Atelectasis is the collapse of small airways and alveoli that are not being inflated. Diminished sounds without adventitious sounds means air is not reaching the area rather than moving through something.

options.text: Negative nitrogen balance
options.rationale: Negative nitrogen balance means the body is breaking down more protein than it takes in. It is a metabolic effect of immobility, not a respiratory one.
